BEGINNER1. What are Union Types?

Definition

A union type describes a value that can be one of several types, written with a pipe | between each option.

Real-world analogy: A union type is like a form field that accepts "phone number OR email" — the value must be exactly one of the listed options, never something outside that set. 
let id: string | number;

id = "abc123";   // ✅ OK
id = 42;         // ✅ OK
// id = true;    // ❌ Error: Type 'boolean' is not assignable

Unions in Function Parameters

function printId(id: string | number) {
    console.log(`Your ID is: ${id}`);
}

printId(101);         // Your ID is: 101
printId("A-102");     // Your ID is: A-102

BEGINNER2. Working with Union Values

TypeScript only lets you use members that exist on every type in the union, until you narrow it down.

function formatId(id: string | number) {
    // id.toUpperCase();   // ❌ Error: 'toUpperCase' doesn't exist on 'number'
    // id.toFixed(2);      // ❌ Error: 'toFixed' doesn't exist on 'string'

    console.log(id.toString());   // ✅ OK - both types have toString()
}

Narrowing with typeof

function formatId(id: string | number): string {
    if (typeof id === "string") {
        return id.toUpperCase();   // ✅ narrowed to string
    }
    return id.toFixed(0);          // ✅ narrowed to number
}

formatId("abc");   // "ABC"
formatId(42);       // "42"
💡 Tip: This "narrow before using" requirement is the same safety mechanism that protects unknown. It forces you to handle every possibility explicitly instead of guessing.

INTERMEDIATE3. Union Types with Objects

interface Cat {
    kind: "cat";
    meow(): void;
}

interface Dog {
    kind: "dog";
    bark(): void;
}

type Pet = Cat | Dog;

function speak(pet: Pet) {
    if (pet.kind === "cat") {
        pet.meow();   // ✅ narrowed to Cat
    } else {
        pet.bark();   // ✅ narrowed to Dog
    }
}

Arrays of Union Types

type Shape =
    | { kind: "circle"; radius: number }
    | { kind: "square"; side: number };

const shapes: Shape[] = [
    { kind: "circle", radius: 5 },
    { kind: "square", side: 4 }
];

INTERMEDIATE4. What are Intersection Types?

An intersection type combines multiple types into one, requiring the value to satisfy all of them simultaneously, written with an ampersand &.

type Named = { name: string };
type Aged = { age: number };

type Person = Named & Aged;

const person: Person = { name: "Kim", age: 34 };
// const invalid: Person = { name: "Kim" };   // ❌ Error: missing 'age'
Real-world analogy: An intersection type is like a job posting that requires "5 years experience AND a CS degree AND a driver's license" — every requirement must be met at once, not just one of them.

Intersecting More Than Two Types

type Identifiable = { id: number };
type Timestamped = { createdAt: Date };
type Named2 = { name: string };

type Record1 = Identifiable & Timestamped & Named2;

const record: Record1 = { id: 1, createdAt: new Date(), name: "Log entry" };

INTERMEDIATE5. Combining Interfaces via Intersection

interface Serializable {
    serialize(): string;
}

interface Comparable {
    compareTo(other: T): number;
}

type Sortable = Serializable & Comparable;

class Money implements Sortable {
    constructor(private cents: number) {}

    serialize(): string {
        return `$${(this.cents / 100).toFixed(2)}`;
    }

    compareTo(other: Money): number {
        return this.cents - other.cents;
    }
}
💡 Tip: Intersections work naturally with type aliases to merge behavior contracts. You could achieve something similar with interface Foo extends A, B, but intersections are more flexible for combining arbitrary types, including primitives and unions.

ADVANCED6. Discriminated Unions

A discriminated union is a union of object types that share a common literal property (the "discriminant" or "tag"), letting TypeScript narrow the exact variant with a simple check.

type Result =
    | { status: "success"; data: string }
    | { status: "error"; message: string }
    | { status: "loading" };

function render(result: Result): string {
    switch (result.status) {
        case "success":
            return `Data: ${result.data}`;      // ✅ narrowed - data exists
        case "error":
            return `Error: ${result.message}`;  // ✅ narrowed - message exists
        case "loading":
            return "Loading...";
    }
}

Exhaustiveness Checking with never

function render(result: Result): string {
    switch (result.status) {
        case "success":
            return `Data: ${result.data}`;
        case "error":
            return `Error: ${result.message}`;
        case "loading":
            return "Loading...";
        default:
            // If a new variant is added to Result and not handled above,
            // this line will fail to compile because 'result' won't be 'never'.
            const exhaustiveCheck: never = result;
            return exhaustiveCheck;
    }
}
Real-world use case: Discriminated unions are the standard TypeScript pattern for modeling API response states (loading / success / error), Redux actions, and parsed AST nodes.

ADVANCED7. Union vs Intersection - Choosing Correctly

Aspect Union (A | B) Intersection (A & B)
Meaning Value is A OR B Value is A AND B
Members you can access Only what's common to all members Everything from every combined type
Typical use case Function accepts multiple input shapes; state machines Mixing in shared behavior; combining role-based fields
Requires narrowing to use fully ✅ Yes ❌ No — everything is available immediately

Conflicting Property Types in Intersections

type A = { value: string };
type B = { value: number };

type Combined = A & B;
// 'value' becomes type 'string & number', which is effectively 'never'
// since no value can be both a string and a number simultaneously

// const x: Combined = { value: "text" };   // ❌ Error

ADVANCED8. Distributive Conditional Behavior with Unions

When a union type is passed through a conditional type, TypeScript applies the conditional to each member individually and unions the results — this is called distribution.

type ToArray = T extends any ? T[] : never;

type Result1 = ToArray;
// Distributes to: ToArray | ToArray
// Result1 = string[] | number[]  (NOT (string | number)[])
⚠️ Common Pitfall: This distribution can be surprising. Wrapping the type parameter in a tuple ([T] extends [any] ? T[] : never) disables distribution when you actually want the union treated as one unit.

ADVANCED9. Common Pitfalls with Unions and Intersections

Pitfall 1: Forgetting to Narrow

function getLength(value: string | string[]) {
    // return value.length;   // Actually works here since both have .length,
    //                           but subtler cases will fail without narrowing
    if (Array.isArray(value)) {
        return value.length;
    }
    return value.length;
}

Pitfall 2: Overlapping Discriminant Values

// ❌ Bad - both variants use the same literal value for 'type'
type Event =
    | { type: "click"; x: number }
    | { type: "click"; y: number };   // duplicate discriminant, narrowing breaks

Pitfall 3: Accidentally Creating never via Intersection

type StringOnly = { id: string };
type NumberOnly = { id: number };

// type Broken = StringOnly & NumberOnly;   // id becomes 'never' - unusable

ADVANCED10. Best Practices

1. Use Discriminated Unions for State Modeling

// ✅ Good
type AsyncState =
    | { status: "idle" }
    | { status: "loading" }
    | { status: "success"; data: T }
    | { status: "error"; error: string };

2. Always Narrow Before Accessing Non-Shared Members

// ✅ Good
if (typeof value === "string") { /* use string members */ }

3. Use Intersections to Compose Small Reusable Pieces

// ✅ Good
type WithId = { id: string };
type WithTimestamps = { createdAt: Date; updatedAt: Date };
type Entity = WithId & WithTimestamps;

4. Add an Exhaustiveness Check on Every Discriminated Union switch

// ✅ Good - catches missing cases when the union grows
default: {
    const _exhaustive: never = value;
    throw new Error(`Unhandled case: ${_exhaustive}`);
}

5. Watch for never When Intersecting Conflicting Primitives

// ❌ Avoid intersecting types with the same key but incompatible primitive types

📋 Quick Reference Summary

Concept Key Points
Union (A | B) Value is one of several types; must narrow to access non-shared members
Intersection (A & B) Value satisfies all combined types simultaneously
Discriminated union Shared literal "tag" property enables precise narrowing via switch/if
Exhaustiveness check Assign to never in the default case to catch unhandled variants
Conflicting intersections Same key with incompatible primitive types collapses to never
Distribution Conditional types distribute over naked union type parameters
